text: I'm a final year CS student at Bennett University. Besides the internship, I built Relay, a project that lets me control my laptop from my phone over WebSockets through a small relay server I wrote.
Got it. What does Relay actually do under the hood — what runs on the laptop, what runs on the phone, and what's the relay server's role?

A small desktop agent runs on the laptop and the phone app is a thin client. Both connect out to my relay server, authenticate over HTTP and upgrade to a WebSocket, and the relay forwards commands from the phone to the agent and results back.
Makes sense. Why route through a relay server instead of connecting the phone directly to the laptop?

text: Take your time — whenever you're ready, start with what the Portal had to do and why you went with micro-frontends at all.

We split the portal into a shell and remotes owned by different teams, loaded with Module Federation so each could deploy independently. The hardest part was shared dependencies, because two remotes pulling different React versions broke hooks, so we pinned singletons for React and the router.
That's the crux — shared singletons. Say a shared library like the router needs a version bump; how do you roll that out without breaking one of the remotes that hasn't updated yet?
